title: Generic functions, classes, and interfaces
hook: Generic type parameters let one function or class work across types while preserving the relationship between input and output — identity<T>(x: T): T is safer than identity(x: any): any.

blocks.text: **Generics** declare type parameters in angle brackets: `function wrap<T>(value: T): T[]`, `class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} }`, `interface Repository<T> { get(id: string): Promise<T | null> }`. The compiler **substitutes** concrete types at each call site — `wrap(42)` infers `T` as `number`. Unlike `any`, generics preserve type flow: `const xs = wrap('hi')` is `string[]`, not `any[]`. Multiple parameters: `function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B]`.

entries.plainDefinition: Placeholder type T declared on function, class, or interface.
Compiler deduces T from arguments without explicit angle brackets.
Replacing T with concrete type at a call site.
Interface with type params — implemented by classes or object literals.
entries.example: interface Cache<T> { get(k: string): T | undefined }

blocks.text: Every utility — `Array<T>`, `Promise<T>`, React `useState<T>`, ORM repositories — is built on generics. Without them you duplicate functions per type or fall back to `any`. C# generics are reified at runtime; TypeScript generics erase completely. Senior interviews ask about inference vs explicit type args, generic methods on classes, and why `function f<T>(x: T): T` beats overloads for simple cases.

blocks.title: When explicit <T>
blocks.body: Provide explicit type args when inference fails — empty arrays, null initial values, or widening literals.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Name the type parameter
items.body: T for single unknown; meaningful names TEntity, TKey for clarity.

items.title: Use T in params and return
items.body: Preserve relationship — input type flows to output.

items.title: Let inference work
items.body: Omit <T> at call site when arguments carry type info.

items.title: Add constraints when needed
items.body: T extends Foo when you must call methods on T — see constraints topic.

blocks.title: Using any instead of T
blocks.body: function bad(x: any): any loses relationship — use T.

blocks.title: Too many type parameters
blocks.body: If T only appears once, you may not need a generic — use concrete type or unknown.

blocks.text: Generic functions can have their own `<T>` separate from outer class `T`. **const type parameters** `function foo<const T>(x: T)` preserve literals. **Generic arrow functions** need `<T,>` trailing comma in TSX: `const f = <T,>(x: T) => x`. Overloads vs generics: overloads for distinct signatures; generics for uniform type families. Declaration files use generics extensively — understanding instantiation helps read @types packages.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot write identity<T>. Thinking generics exist at runtime in TS. Using any when T would work.

interviewTakeaways: Generics preserve input-output type relationships — unlike any.
Inference from arguments; explicit <T> when inference fails.
Classes, functions, interfaces all support <T> — constraints unlock members.
60s: T is a placeholder substituted per call site. Erased at emit. identity<T>(x:T):T preserves type. Use constraints when calling methods on T.
Follow-up: default type params, const type params, generic methods on classes.
commonPitfalls: Weak: "generics are runtime types in TS" — erased on emit.
any instead of T in simple wrappers.
Strong: "Generics parameterize types at compile time. Inference from args. Constraints for operations on T."

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS functions accept any value — TS generics add compile-time type parameterization without runtime cost.
C# List<T> exists at runtime; TS T[] is Array with erased T — same syntax spirit, different runtime model.
